messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet Nguyen is a twenty-two-year-old Vietnamese-American UX designer who presents with a PCL-5 score of 56 following a devastating earthquake that struck while he was visiting extended family in central Vietnam eighteen months ago. The quake hit without warning in the early morning, collapsing part of the house around him. He remembers the particular pressure of a ceiling beam across the back of his neck, the acrid taste of plaster dust filling his mouth, and the sound of his aunt calling his name from somewhere he could not locate in the dark. Several family members were injured; one did not survive. He was evacuated within hours, but the event left a mark on him that has not loosened its grip.

In the weeks that followed his return to the United States, Kiet noticed that certain experiences seemed to reach directly into that morning and pull it forward. A stiff neck after long hours at his workstation — entirely ordinary for someone who spends his days arranging wireframes and prototyping interfaces — would arrive as something else entirely: the pressure of the beam, the dust on his tongue, the sense that the walls were still moving. The somatic pain in his neck functions as one of the most reliable triggers he knows, and when it fires, the memory does not return as a coherent narrative so much as an atmosphere — taste without image, dread without scene, the full emotional weight of the event arriving before any picture forms. He has described sitting at his desk, feeling suddenly and inexplicably ill, the nausea and physical unwellness spreading through him, and finding himself back in that collapsed room without being able to say exactly how he got there. Hearing colleagues mention anything adjacent to the disaster — a news segment about flooding, a conversation about structural damage — operates the same way, the triggers pulling the memory forward with a force that feels disproportionate and humiliating.

What troubles Kiet as much as the intrusions themselves is what they seem to confirm about the world. Each time the memory surfaces — fragmentary, overwhelming, tasting of plaster — he finds it harder to hold onto any stable sense of his surroundings or the people in them. The memory carries a quality of unreality that has seeped outward: the event was so extreme, so far outside anything he had been prepared for, that he has come to feel that ordinary life is a kind of performance, and that people around him are similarly performing a safety they do not actually possess. He has grown convinced that people are not what they seem — that the colleagues who laugh easily at lunch, the friends who make weekend plans, are either unaware of how fragile everything is or are concealing it. This appraisal of others as unknowable and fundamentally unreliable has in turn narrowed his world considerably. He avoids team social events at the design agency where he works, declines invitations, and has stopped visiting the gym where he used to train, partly because the physical exertion reliably produces neck tension that he cannot trust not to trigger him. The avoidance has not gone unnoticed: his manager recently commented on his withdrawal from collaborative sessions, and a close friend from college stopped reaching out after several unanswered messages.

The sense that people cannot be trusted has itself become a source of new triggers. Moments of social friction — a misread message, a colleague's ambiguous expression — now carry a charge they did not before, confirming his belief that he does not belong among people who have not been through what he has. He has come to feel isolated and set apart in a way that feels permanent rather than circumstantial, and more recently he has begun to feel that he no longer belongs anywhere at all — not in the United States, where the disaster feels unreal to everyone around him, and not in Vietnam, which he associates entirely with what happened. This sense of belonging nowhere has made ordinary life feel like an extended waiting room, and the isolation itself keeps him alert for signs of threat, so that even benign physical sensations or passing references to disaster pull the memory forward again.

What finally brought Kiet to seek help was a presentation at work he could not complete — he had been storyboarding a user journey when a colleague mentioned an earthquake in the news, and he left the room and did not return. He is most afraid that nothing will feel real or safe again. What he hopes, cautiously, is that someone can help him understand why he cannot simply leave that morning behind.
